source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: error analysis section
finding: LINC's own error analysis names three failure modes: L1 missing implicit information, L2 explicit info mis-encoded, L3 syntax errors. Syntax errors fall with model strength. LINC predicts Uncertain far more than CoT, so translation loss turns into false Uncertain.
numbers: L3 syntax errors across generations: StarCoder+ 38%, GPT-3.5 24%, GPT-4 13%. GPT-4 on FOLIO: LINC predicts 24% True, 17% False, 57% Uncertain (2% error); CoT predicts 32% / 27% / 41%. Pairwise misprediction similarity LINC vs other methods 0.14, 0.21, 0.22; among the in-context methods 0.52-0.56.
quote: LINC predicts Uncertain much more frequently than CoT (57% vs. 41%)
limits: Hand-checked small FOLIO validation set; GPT-4 (2023) is not a 2025 model. Most common syntax error is one symbol used with different arities.
agent_relevance: Translation is the bottleneck, and its errors are lossy (drops to Uncertain), not random. LINC and CoT make different mistakes, so a router or vote over both can add value.

source: Sun et al. (2024) GFaiR: Resolution refutation for NL logic reasoning
finding: A step-wise reasoner that adds resolution refutation (negate hypothesis, resolve to contradiction) is complete for FOL where forward/backward chaining is not. It stays accurate at depth 5 where forward-chaining reasoners drop.
numbers: RuleTaker depth-5, entailment/full accuracy: GFaiR 94.2 / 91.9; FaiRR (forward chaining) 78.7 / 67.8; NLProofs 69.6 / 57.3. Depth 3: GFaiR 99.5 / 99.5 vs FaiRR 98.4 / 96.0.
limits: Trained XLNet/T5 modules, not a prompted LLM. Table text extracted from a two-column PDF; row alignment inferred from the depth trend. ChatGPT baseline had full accuracy 2.7 on Hard RuleTaker.
agent_relevance: Refutation (negate the goal, then look for contradiction) is the resolution idea that carries over to a scaffold. It also fixes the completeness gap of pure forward chaining, which is the gap a one-direction agent has.

source: Qi et al. (2025) ProverQA via ProverGen, ICLR 2025
finding: On a prover-verified FOL benchmark with long proofs and distractors, strong LLMs with CoT reach only about 50% on the hard split. CoT helps easy problems much more than hard ones.
numbers: GPT-4o CoT: easy 94.20, medium 79.40, hard 50.00; Claude-3.5-Sonnet CoT: 95.20 / 83.60 / 56.40; Mistral-Large CoT hard 52.20. GPT-4o standard prompting hard 46.20, so CoT gain on hard is +3.8 vs +7.0 on easy. ProntoQA CoT GPT-4o 100.00.
limits: GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 era models. Hard split proofs are long. Not a test of saturation.
agent_relevance: Depth beyond about 5 steps is where plain CoT stops working in this data. This is the zone where a scaffold with queues and a verifier could matter. No study ties this to Haken-style proof-size limits.

source: Qi et al. (2025) ProverQA ablation on distraction and order
finding: Removing irrelevant premises and ordering premises along the proof both raise GPT-4o's CoT accuracy, most on hard problems. So selection of relevant facts is a measured cost.
numbers: GPT-4o CoT hard: default 50.00; no distractions 57.40 (+7.4); no distractions and ordered premises 62.40 (+12.4). Medium 79.40 -> 82.20 -> 87.40. Easy 94.20 -> 94.40 -> 95.60.
limits: One model, one benchmark. Order here was set to match the proof, which a real agent does not know.
agent_relevance: The loss from distractors and bad order is the same job a clause-selection loop does (pick the relevant item next). A 12-point hard-set gap is an upper bound on what better step selection could win for CoT-style agents.

finding: In LLM search, pure best-first (always expand the highest LLM-scored node) over-exploits and collapses on hard instances, while letting the LLM decide when to explore or continue wins. This is an LLM analogue of a greedy weight queue without an age queue.
numbers: Win rate % (GPT-4o): Countdown diff 7: BestFS 11.11, MCTS 32.63, LFS 47.37; diff 5: BestFS 49.47, MCTS 60.00, LFS 63.16. Sudoku 4x4: BestFS 41.05, MCTS(C=0.5) 100, LFS 96.84. o3-mini Countdown diff 7: BestFS 13.33, MCTS 41.05, LFS 78.95. Sudoku 6x6 o3-mini: LFS 25.26.
quote: BestFS ... does not balance exploitation and exploration sufficiently
limits: Only Countdown and Sudoku; MCTS result depends on its constant C (C=1.0 on Sudoku 4x4 gave 2.22). Not a given-clause design; no age queue was tested.
agent_relevance: Closest measured evidence for gaps 1, 2 and 7: greedy best-first without a fairness mechanism is much worse on deep problems. It does not test an age:weight mix itself.

source: Herr et al. (2025) LLM-First Search, efficiency
finding: Area under the performance profile ranks the self-guided search first on win rate and on win rate per token, with the gap growing for the stronger model.
numbers: AUP win rate GPT-4o: ToT-BFS 4.06, BestFS 5.98, MCTS 7.09, LFS 8.99; o3-mini: BestFS 4.23, MCTS 6.00, LFS 7.20. Efficiency score GPT-4o: BestFS 2.67, MCTS 3.68, LFS 4.70; o3-mini: MCTS 5.61, LFS 7.20.
limits: Tokens counted as average per game; two puzzle tasks only.
agent_relevance: Gives a token-fair comparison design (win rate and win rate per token) that a given-clause agent test can copy.

source: CLOVER (2025) compositional FOL translation with solver verification, ICLR 2025
finding: With GPT-4o, translation (not solving) limits Logic-LM; breaking sentences into sub-formulas and checking equivalence with SAT raises program accuracy a lot, most on the hardest task. First translation-versus-solver split on a GPT-4-class model found.
numbers: GPT-4o, Logic-LM vs CLOVER: AR-LSAT program accuracy 17.3 vs 46.8, execution rate 33.8 vs 59.7, execution accuracy (of executable) 51.3 vs 78.3. Logic-LM translation accuracy falls as formula complexity rises (Fig. 1a, five complexity bins); CLOVER's largest gain is in the highest bin. Logic-LM on FOLIO execution accuracy 94.2 vs CLOVER 92.7.
quote: LLM performs first-order logic translation faithfully to a certain degree of complexity but falls short beyond that limit
limits: Table text from two-column PDF; the AR-LSAT row is read from the first line of Table 2. Same authors' method, own reproductions of Logic-LM.
agent_relevance: Logic-LM translates only 33.8% of AR-LSAT problems into runnable code and the runnable ones are right 51.3% of the time. Both stages lose, and the loss grows with formula complexity. Translation, not solving, dominates.

finding: Some translation errors are logically consistent, so a solver cannot flag them; only an independent check of meaning catches them. This limits the self-refinement from solver error messages seen in Logic-LM.
numbers: Logic-LM gets execution accuracy of 51.3% on AR-LSAT even when the program runs.
quote: LLM sometimes make logically consistent translation errors
limits: Argument from one paper; the paper's own fix is SAT-based equivalence checks.
agent_relevance: Solver success is not evidence of faithful translation. A stop rule that treats solver proved as final needs a faithfulness check (a G-type guardrail).

source: LOGICPO (2025) NL to FOL translation with preference optimisation
finding: Small models fine-tuned (SFT then KTO) to translate NL to FOL cut syntax errors sharply and beat GPT-3.5/GPT-4 LINC pipelines on FOLIO logical correctness. Error counts give a translation-error breakdown.
numbers: FOLIO logical correctness: GPT-4 LINC 4-shot 45.82, Phi-3.5 Mini SFT+KTO 61.52 (overall F1 64.43); GPT-3.5 LINC 8-shot about 7 points below Phi-3.5 SFT. Error counts on FOLIO (L1 implicit loss / L2 explicit / L3 syntax / wrong translation): Logic-LM GPT-3.5 18 / 20 / 84 / 4; LINC GPT-3.5 22 / 13 / 36 / 1; Llama-3 8B 10 / 15 / 14 / 9; Phi-3.5 13 / 20 / 14 / 1. Syntax errors down 83.33% vs Logic-LM and 61.11% vs LINC. ProofWriter 65.28, ProntoQA 89.0 logical correctness.
limits: Their own manual annotation, small counts, FOLIO validation. Baseline numbers are from earlier papers, not re-run. Author list not recorded.
agent_relevance: After syntax is removed, L1 and L2 (meaning loss) remain at 25-40 cases; so a repair loop that only reads solver errors cannot fix them. Supports a verify-the-meaning step.

finding: A curated memory of past solutions used at test time lifts strong models a lot on tasks with repeatable tricks, but small models gain little because their memory fills with wrong entries. Closest LLM analogue to the looped learning in ENIGMA (gap 8).
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23% to 50%, AIME 2025 +30%; GPT-4o Game of 24 about 10% to 99% once it stored a Python solution; GPQA-Diamond +9% for Claude; MMLU-Pro Engineering/Physics up to +8%. GPT-4o-mini and Haiku gained only limited amounts.
quote: DC is not a panacea. We found that smaller models, such as GPT-4o-mini, benefit from DC in limited amounts.
limits: Gains depend on reusable code and tricks (Game of 24). Retrieval ranks by similarity of past inputs. Single group, no replication seen.
agent_relevance: Past-trace reuse works only when the model can already produce good solutions, so the loop needs a quality gate. Like ENIGMA, it needs seed proofs. No saturation curve was found in the text read, so when it saturates stays open.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? Overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models repeat solutions after the first correct one. Later solutions add little accuracy and little diversity. Trimming repeats cut tokens about half with no accuracy loss. A measured LLM analogue of redundancy elimination (gap 6).
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview: 1,953% more tokens than conventional models for 2+3; 13 solutions for that question; 2 to 4 solution rounds in 76-80% of QwQ cases (59-63% for DeepSeek-R1); first solution gives most accuracy; self-training that removes redundant solutions cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept.
quote: Subsequent solutions ... contribute minimally to accuracy improvement
limits: Open-weight o1-like models only, math sets (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). It removes whole repeated solutions, not step-level subsumption.
agent_relevance: Dedupe of whole re-derivations is cheap and safe on easy problems. Cutting too early on hard problems is untested here, so keep budget for second looks on hard items.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) neural clause selection in Vampire (carried from earlier read)
finding: Carried from the cross-check: gains are large on single strategies and smaller in portfolios; no LLM is used as clause selector there, only small nets.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Not re-opened in this step.
agent_relevance: Relevant to gap 5: the newest prover-side paper found still uses small networks, not LLMs.

source: Search record: LLM-guided clause selection in E or Vampire (2 web searches; arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs rate limited)
finding: Web searches returned no paper where an LLM selects given clauses inside E or Vampire. All clause-guidance work found uses trees, GNNs or small transformers (ENIGMA, Suda, Chvalovsky). Negative result, not proof of absence.
numbers: 0 papers found among about 20 titles scanned. Results included Suda 2021 (arXiv 2102.03529) and the LPAR-26 Chvalovsky et al. paper.
limits: Search budget was spent; the APIs returned HTTP 429 in this run. Papers after mid-2025 may exist.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open. A fair test needs an LLM scorer cheap enough for the prover time limit; ENIGMA and Suda data say speed decides.

source: Search record: LLM agent with age and weight step queues vs best-first (web search)
finding: No study was found that gives an LLM agent separate age and weight queues for step selection. Nearest are LLM-First Search (d05) and Natural Language Deduction through Search over Statement Compositions (2201.06028, not read). Negative result.
limits: Absence of evidence from a limited search.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2 stay open; the design needs a first test. d05 gives the baseline shape and metric.

source: Bostrom et al. (2022) Natural Language Deduction through Search over Statement Compositions
finding: Search over LLM-composed statements with a learned scorer for which statements to compose next: the closest NL version of a given-clause loop with a learned scorer. Only the file was fetched; findings not extracted this session.
limits: Not read in detail this session.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a follow-up read before any design claim about step-selection heuristics.
